title: Why I Left Systems Engineering for Grad School
excerpt: After three years of writing C++ at NetApp, I decided to trade a comfortable SWE role for a master's degree. Here's what pushed me over the edge.
body:
After three years of writing C++ at NetApp, I decided to trade a comfortable SWE role for a master's degree. Here's what pushed me over the edge.

I loved the work — optimizing RAID layouts, reducing downtime, squeezing out storage capacity. But I kept gravitating toward the AI papers my teammates shared in Slack. I'd spend weekends building toy models while my day job was firmware. The gap between what I was doing and what I wanted to be doing kept growing.

Grad school wasn't the safe choice. I gave up a solid salary, moved across the country, and went back to being a student. But within the first semester at SJSU, I was knee-deep in deep learning, distributed systems, and building things I actually dreamed about. Sometimes the uncomfortable path is the right one.

title: Building a Dead Man's Switch with Twilio and ElevenLabs
excerpt: How we built a tiered escalation system that makes automated phone calls with AI-generated voices when someone stops checking in.
body:
How we built a tiered escalation system that makes automated phone calls with AI-generated voices when someone stops checking in.

For AMBER, our covert DV evidence platform, we needed a failsafe — if a user stops responding, something has gone wrong. We designed a three-tier escalation: first a text, then a call with a pre-written script read by ElevenLabs TTS, then a full emergency alert with victim demographics sent to pre-approved contacts.

The tricky part was timing. APScheduler runs cron-style sweeps every 10 seconds, checking for missed check-ins. We had to handle edge cases like timezone drift, network failures, and the user simply forgetting their phone. False positives in this context aren't just annoying — they're dangerous.

The system works. It shipped. And I hope no one ever needs to use it.

title: The Clamp Function Changed How I Think About CSS
excerpt: Forget media queries for font sizes. One CSS function replaced dozens of breakpoints in my portfolio site.
body:
Forget media queries for font sizes. One CSS function replaced dozens of breakpoints in my portfolio site.

I used to write three or four font-size declarations per heading — one for mobile, tablet, desktop, and sometimes ultrawide. Then I discovered clamp(). The syntax is simple: clamp(min, preferred, max). The preferred value uses viewport units, so the font scales fluidly between the min and max bounds.

For example, text-[clamp(1.2rem, 3vw, 2rem)] gives you a heading that's never smaller than 1.2rem, never larger than 2rem, and smoothly scales in between. No breakpoints. No jumps. Just fluid typography.

I went through my entire site and replaced every responsive font-size stack with a single clamp(). The CSS got shorter, the visual result got smoother, and I stopped worrying about that one weird tablet width where everything looked off.

title: What Three Years of RAID Taught Me About Failure
excerpt: Working on storage systems at NetApp taught me that failure isn't a bug — it's a feature you design around.
body:
Working on storage systems at NetApp taught me that failure isn't a bug — it's a feature you design around.

In RAID, disks fail. That's not a possibility, it's a certainty. The entire architecture is built on the assumption that hardware will break. Parity bits, hot spares, rebuild algorithms — everything exists because someone said 'this will fail, so what happens next?'

I carried this mindset into every project since. When I design a system now, my first question isn't 'how does this work?' — it's 'how does this break?' What happens when the API is down? When the user closes the tab mid-save? When two people edit the same record?

The best engineers I worked with at NetApp didn't write code that never failed. They wrote code that failed gracefully. There's a huge difference.

title: Agentic AI Is Not Just a Buzzword
excerpt: After building three multi-agent systems, here's what I actually learned about when agents work — and when they don't.
body:
After building three multi-agent systems, here's what I actually learned about when agents work — and when they don't.

Everyone's talking about agentic AI. Most of the discourse is hype. But after shipping TravelPlanner, AMBER, and Transitly — all built on multi-agent architectures — I have opinions grounded in real production pain.

Agents work when you have genuinely separable concerns. In AMBER, the Ingest agent doesn't need to know about legal document formatting. The Legal agent doesn't care about media understanding. They each have a clear job, a clear input, and a clear output. LangGraph lets you wire them together without spaghetti.

Agents don't work when you use them as a substitute for thinking. I've seen people spin up five agents for a task that should be one function call. The orchestration overhead, the token cost, the debugging complexity — it's not free. Every agent boundary is a potential failure point.

My rule of thumb: if you can draw the agent graph on a napkin and each node has a one-sentence job description, you're probably fine. If you need a flowchart to explain the flowchart, simplify.
